world.bio: I grew up above my parents' bakery on Mott Street and now work as a freelance Cantonese–English court interpreter in Brooklyn and Manhattan. My grandmother speaks Taishanese and I grew up translating for her at the doctor's, which is how I started. Since remote interpreting took over my bookings have dropped, so I have more free evenings than I am used to.
skills_assets: Court-certified Cantonese-English interpreter, working in criminal, family and housing courts
Fluent in Cantonese, Mandarin, English; understands Taishanese and Toishan-flavoured Cantonese because of my grandmother
Interpreter training at Hunter College, glossary files for legal and medical vocabulary
Quiet home office with a good headset and a second laptop for remote sessions
A Thursday pottery class and a small kiln-fired collection of lopsided bowls

projects.name: Remote interpreting transition
projects.text: Since the courts expanded remote interpreting, my court bookings dropped by a third. Evenings used to be for prep, now they are mostly free. I am applying to a couple of agencies for remote hearings but the pay per hour is lower. I have not decided whether to adapt fully or look for something different.

projects.name: Thursday pottery class
projects.text: I signed up in June at a studio in Gowanus. I am making a set of rice bowls that I hope will not look like I made them with my feet. The teacher says my walls are too thick.

notes.text: Court was empty-ish today. Two hearings cancelled, one moved to video. I sat in the hallway of the Kings County courthouse with a coffee and watched the other interpreters walking in and out. Half of them look as tired as I feel. One said, 'It was never like this ten years ago.'

Dad called. He is selling the bakery building. He did not say it that way, he said 'we are thinking about the future.' I said which future. He said the one where he does not climb stairs at 4 a.m. I said that is fair. Then I went into the bathroom and cried for a bit.

Pottery class Thursday. I made a bowl that collapsed on the wheel. The teacher said that is how you learn where the wall is too thin. Everyone else at the table has been doing this for years. I did not mind. It is nice to be bad at something with no consequences.

Spent the whole evening free. Used to be I would be preparing for tomorrow's cases, glossary files open, the legal terms laid out. Instead I rewatched an old Hong Kong drama with the subtitles on. It made me feel nostalgic for the days when my grandmother sat next to me and corrected my Cantonese.

Visited Ah Po on Saturday. She told me the same story about the typhoon in Taishan that I have heard a hundred times. This time I wrote it down. Her Taishanese has words I cannot find in any dictionary. I am afraid that when she goes those words go with her.
An agency recruiter emailed me about remote video sessions, $38 an hour for phone, $42 for video. Court pays me $70-ish per hour. The numbers are dispiriting.

Walked through Chinatown after lunch. All the old shops are different now. The bakery two doors down from Mom and Dad's closed. Another dessert shop opened. Prices of everything are up. I picked up a pineapple bun and it tasted fine and not the same.
Looking at flights to Guangzhou for the spring. I want to take Ah Po back to Taishan if she is well enough. She has not been in twenty years. I have not been in ten. I am scared she will say no.
Finished my second bowl. It is thick, but it holds water. I put a plant in it. It sits next to my laptop and I look at it a lot.

messages.text:
Marcus: Linda, the 10:30 is going remote. Can you do the video link?
Me: I can, but I need a stable connection. Is the court WiFi okay?
Marcus: Honestly, not really. Do it from home.

Dad: Come for dinner Sunday. Your mom is making fish.
Me: Sure.
Dad: We need to talk about something.
Me: I know.

Jen: How is work?
Me: Slow. I have free evenings now.
Jen: Come to the dumpling night then!
Me: Maybe next week.

Recruiter: We have a Cantonese-English remote role at $38/hr. Interested?
Me: Thanks, can I think about it?
Recruiter: Of course. It closes Friday.

Ah Po (voice note): Lin-lin, wan sik fan mei? (Have you eaten?)
Me: Sik jyun la. (Yes.) How are you feeling?
Ah Po: Hou hou. Gwai-jat lai tong ngo king-gai la. (Fine. Come chat with me sometime.)

calendar.event: Sunday dinner at parents' (bakery building conversation)
Visit Ah Po, record some stories

relations.about: Taishanese-speaking, 89, lives with her son in Flushing
Selling the bakery building; tired but proud
Old school friend, keeps inviting her out

constraints: Court work is confidential, I cannot discuss cases
Weekdays during court hours I am unavailable
Pay below $35/hr is not worth it
Evenings are open but I am protective of my Thursday class
sensitive: Worried about money, savings are thinner than people think
Feels guilty for not being around more for her grandmother
Her father has not told the rest of the family how bad the bakery's finances are
